chunks: Open-drain and push-pull meaning. The question: What does open-drain/push-pull mean?
Push-pull and open-drain describe how an output pin is built from transistors, which are electrically controlled switches. A push-pull output has two switches.
One pushes the pin up to the supply and the other pulls it down to ground, so the pin is always firmly driven. An open-drain output has only the pull-down switch.
For a high level it simply lets go, and an outside resistor pulls the pin up.
Think of a window blind. A push-pull blind has a motor that rolls it up and rolls it down. An open-drain blind has only a cord that pulls it down.
When you let go, a spring in the roller lifts it, but that spring is something you supply, not part of the cord. The spring is the pull-up resistor.
Left, push-pull: the shared gate drive turns exactly one of MP and MN on. Right, open-drain: only MN.
The resistor Rpu is external to the chip, so the pin's high level is a property of the board , not of the chip.
Push-pull: an output with two switches, one driving high and one driving low. Open-drain: an output with only a pull-down switch.
The transistor's output end, called the drain, is left unconnected ("open") inside the chip.
Pull-up resistor: the outside resistor that supplies the high level for an open-drain pin. Released state: the pull-down switch is off, so the pin is not driven at all.
Wired-AND: several open-drain outputs on one line. The line is low if any one of them pulls low.
Take a 3. 3 volts pin. As push-pull, writing 1 turns the top switch on and the pin sits near 3. 3 volts. Writing 0 turns the bottom switch on and the pin sits near 0 volts.
As open-drain with a 4. 7 kilohms pull-up, writing 0 turns the bottom switch on. If that switch has 25 ohms, the pin sits at 3. 3 times 25 over 4725 about 0. 02 volts.
Writing 1 releases the pin, and the resistor lifts it to 3. 3 volts. With no pull-up, writing 1 leaves the pin floating. That is the whole idea.
"Push-pull means the output has two transistors: a PMOS that pushes the pin up to VDD and an NMOS that pulls it to ground, so it actively drives both high and low.
Open-drain means there's only the NMOS, and its drain is left open: it can pull the pin low, or release it. To get a high you need an external pull-up resistor.
So push-pull is fast and needs nothing else, while open-drain needs a resistor but lets several outputs share a line, with the line low if any one pulls low."
